# Introduction

This project investigates writer information in a simulated handwritten-digit dataset using two neural-network approaches. The first approach uses a convolutional neural network (CNN) to directly predict the identity of the writer. The second uses a Siamese neural network to determine whether two handwriting samples were produced by the same person.

The dataset contains 25,000 images of handwritten digits generated by 20 writers. Each writer completed five independent recording sessions and produced 50 examples of each digit from 0 to 4 in each session. The images have dimensions 28 × 28 pixels. The handwriting is simulated and writing style varies both within and between sessions.

The objectives were to investigate visual variation between writers, digits and sessions, build a CNN for writer identification, construct a Siamese network for same-writer verification, justify train, validation and test splits, conduct limited hyperparameter optimisation, and compare the two approaches.

## Limitations of the simulated data

The data are simulated and therefore cleaner and more controlled than handwriting collected in realistic conditions. Only 20 writers and five digits are represented. Real-world handwriting may also contain scanning artefacts, different pens and paper, varying resolution, incomplete strokes and background noise.

# Train, validation and test strategy


## 2.1 CNN split by session


```{r}
split_cnn <- case_when(
  meta$session %in% 1:3 ~ "train",
  meta$session == 4     ~ "val",
  TRUE                  ~ "test"
)

table(split_cnn, meta$person_id)

idx <- lapply(
  c(train = "train", val = "val", test = "test"),
  function(s) which(split_cnn == s)
)

x_train <- x[idx$train, , , , drop = FALSE]
y_train <- meta$person_id[idx$train] - 1L

x_val <- x[idx$val, , , , drop = FALSE]
y_val <- meta$person_id[idx$val] - 1L

x_test <- x[idx$test, , , , drop = FALSE]
y_test <- meta$person_id[idx$test] - 1L
```
The dataset was split by recording session rather than by writer. Sessions 1–3 were allocated to training, Session 4 to validation, and Session 5 to testing. This strategy was chosen because the objective is to evaluate whether the CNN can recognize the same 20 writers across different recording sessions. A writer-based split would instead assess generalization to writers whose handwriting was not represented during training, which is a different research question.
The training set is used to learn writer-specific handwriting features from labelled images. The validation set contains images from Session 4 and is used to monitor learning and guide model selection, such as choosing hyperparameters or determining when to stop training. The test set contains images from Session 5 and is reserved for the final evaluation after model development is complete.
This strategy evaluates within-writer, across-session generalization. The writer identities are shared across all three subsets, but the recording sessions are separated. Therefore, the evaluation assesses whether the model can identify known writers from a later session, rather than whether it can identify entirely unseen writers.
Potential data leakage could arise if duplicate or highly similar images occur across sessions, or if data-dependent preprocessing uses information from the validation or test sets. Although the session-based split prevents images from the same session being distributed across different subsets, it does not guarantee complete independence between samples. To reduce these risks, image duplication should be checked, learned preprocessing parameters should be estimated from training data only, and Session 5 should not be used for model selection. Using test results repeatedly to modify the model could lead to overly optimistic estimates of generalization performance.



## Random-image baseline split

```{r}
set.seed(2026)

split_rand <- sample(
  c("train", "val", "test"),
  nrow(meta),
  replace = TRUE,
  prob = c(0.6, 0.2, 0.2)
)

table(split_rand)
prop.table(table(split_rand))
```

A random-image split was considered as a baseline, allocating approximately 60% of images to training, 20% to validation, and 20% to testing. This approach allows each subset to potentially contain images from all writers and recording sessions, providing a baseline for comparison with the session-based split.
However, because images are assigned independently, samples from the same writer and session may appear across all three subsets. If handwriting characteristics or image-generation patterns are shared across samples, this could produce optimistic performance estimates. Therefore, this strategy evaluates generalization to randomly held-out images rather than specifically to unseen recording sessions or unseen writers.

#CNN writer identification and tuning

## 3.1 CNN model builder

```{r}
build_cnn <- function(filters = 32,
                      dense_units = 64,
                      dropout = 0.3,
                      lr = 1e-3) {

  model <- keras_model_sequential(
    input_shape = c(28, 28, 1)
  ) |>
    layer_conv_2d(
      filters,
      kernel_size = 3,
      activation = "relu",
      padding = "same"
    ) |>
    layer_max_pooling_2d(pool_size = 2) |>
    layer_conv_2d(
      filters * 2,
      kernel_size = 3,
      activation = "relu",
      padding = "same"
    ) |>
    layer_max_pooling_2d(pool_size = 2) |>
    layer_flatten() |>
    layer_dropout(dropout) |>
    layer_dense(dense_units, activation = "relu") |>
    layer_dense(20, activation = "softmax")

  model |> compile(
    optimizer = optimizer_adam(learning_rate = lr),
    loss = "sparse_categorical_crossentropy",
    metrics = "accuracy"
  )

  model
}
```

## 3.2 CNN Model 1: baseline

```{r}
set_random_seed(2026)

cnn1 <- build_cnn(
  filters = 32,
  dense_units = 64,
  dropout = 0.3,
  lr = 1e-3
)

history1 <- cnn1 |> fit(
  x_train, y_train,
  epochs = 20,
  batch_size = 64,
  validation_data = list(x_val, y_val),
  callbacks = list(
    callback_early_stopping(
      monitor = "val_loss",
      patience = 3,
      restore_best_weights = TRUE

)

plot(history1)
```



Hyperparameter tuning was conducted by comparing four CNN configurations as shown in @tbl-cnn-tuning above, a baseline model and three alternative models. The number of convolutional filters, dense units, dropout rate, and learning rate were varied to assess their effects on validation performance. Model 2 reduced the dense units from 64 to 32 and increased dropout from 0.3 to 0.5. Model 3 further reduced the learning rate from \(10^{-3}\) to \(10^{-4}\), while Model 4 also reduced the number of filters from 32 to 16. The models were evaluated using best validation accuracy and minimum validation loss.
Model 3 performed best, achieving the highest validation accuracy of 61.00% and the lowest validation loss of 1.4424 among the four configurations. Its parameters were 32 filters, 32 dense units, a dropout rate of 0.5, and a learning rate of \(10^{-4}\). These results suggest that the lower learning rate improved performance for this configuration.

The selected CNN model was evaluated on the held-out test set to assess its ability to identify writers from their handwriting. The model achieved an overall classification accuracy of 55.1%, indicating that it correctly identified the writer in approximately half of the test images.

As shown in @tbl-cnn-digit above, classification accuracy varied across the five digits. Digit 1 achieved the highest accuracy at 64.8%, followed by digit 2 at 56.1%, digit 4 at 54.4%, and digit 3 at 53.9%. Digit 0 had the lowest accuracy at 46.3%. These differences suggest that the usefulness of handwriting features for writer identification varied by digit, potentially because some digit shapes provided more distinctive writer-specific characteristics than others.

Performance also varied substantially across individual writers, as shown in @tbl-cnn-writer. Writers 10 and 17 achieved 100% accuracy, while Writer 14 achieved 99.6% and Writer 5 achieved 89.6%. In contrast, Writers 4 and 12 had 0% accuracy, while Writers 19 and 9 achieved only 18.8% and 19.6%, respectively. This variation suggests that the model learned distinctive handwriting patterns for some writers more effectively than for others.

The confusion matrix in @tbl-cnn-confusion provides further insight into these classification errors. The diagonal entries represent correctly classified images, while off-diagonal entries indicate cases where a writer was predicted as another writer. For example, Writer 11 was correctly classified in all 250 test images, whereas all 250 images belonging to Writer 5 were misclassified. Of these, 154 were predicted as Writer 13. Other notable confusion patterns included Writer 10 being predicted as Writer 2 in 200 cases and Writer 13 being predicted as Writer 8 in 82 cases. These patterns suggest that the model struggled to distinguish certain writers, potentially because their handwriting features were similar.


The Siamese split evaluates whether the model can compare handwriting from writers who were not seen during training.

# Siamese network

## Constructing same-writer and different-writer pairs

```{r}
rows <- lapply(
  c(train = "train", val = "val", test = "test"),
  function(s) which(split_sia == s)
)

make_pairs <- function(rows, n, same_digit = TRUE) {

  p <- meta$person_id[rows]
  d <- meta$digit[rows]

  by_pd <- split(rows, paste(p, d))
  by_p <- split(rows, p)
  writers <- unique(p)

  pick <- function(v) v[sample.int(length(v), 1)]

  a <- sample(rows, n, replace = TRUE)
  y <- rep(c(1L, 0L), length.out = n)
  b <- integer(n)

  for (k in seq_len(n)) {
    pa <- meta$person_id[a[k]]
    da <- meta$digit[a[k]]

    if (y[k] == 1L) {
      pool <- if (same_digit) by_pd[[paste(pa, da)]] else by_p[[as.character(pa)]]
      pool <- setdiff(pool, a[k])
    } else {
      pb <- pick(setdiff(writers, pa))
      pool <- if (same_digit) by_pd[[paste(pb, da)]] else by_p[[as.character(pb)]]
    }

    b[k] <- pick(pool)
  }

  tibble(
    a = a,
    b = b,
    y = y,
    digit_a = meta$digit[a],
    digit_b = meta$digit[b],
    sess_a = meta$session[a],
    sess_b = meta$session[b]
  )
}
```

```{r}
set.seed(2026)

pairs <- list(
  train = make_pairs(rows$train, 30000),
  val = make_pairs(rows$val, 6000),
  test = make_pairs(rows$test, 6000)
)

table(pairs$train$y)
table(pairs$val$y)
table(pairs$test$y)
```

Pairs were balanced between same-writer and different-writer examples. The same digit was used in both images of each pair so that the network was encouraged to learn writer style rather than digit identity.

## Convert pairs to model inputs

```{r}
get_xy <- function(pr) {
  list(
    x = list(
      x[pr$a, , , , drop = FALSE],
      x[pr$b, , , , drop = FALSE]
    ),
    y = matrix(pr$y, ncol = 1)
  )
}

tr <- get_xy(pairs$train)
va <- get_xy(pairs$val)
te <- get_xy(pairs$test)
```

## Encoder and contrastive loss

```{r}
build_encoder <- function(emb = 32, filters = 32, dropout = 0.2) {
  keras_model_sequential(
    input_shape = c(28, 28, 1)
  ) |>
    layer_conv_2d(filters, 3, activation = "relu", padding = "same") |>
    layer_max_pooling_2d(2) |>
    layer_conv_2d(filters * 2, 3, activation = "relu", padding = "same") |>
    layer_max_pooling_2d(2) |>
    layer_flatten() |>
    layer_dropout(dropout) |>
    layer_dense(emb)
}

contrastive_loss <- function(margin = 1) {
  function(y_true, y_pred) {
    y_true <- op_cast(y_true, "float32")
    pos <- y_true * op_square(y_pred)
    neg <- (1 - y_true) *
      op_square(op_maximum(margin - y_pred, 0))
    op_mean(pos + neg)
  }
}
```

## Siamese model builder

```{r}
build_siamese <- function(
  emb = 32,
  filters = 32,
  dropout = 0.2,
  margin = 1,
  lr = 1e-3
) {

  encoder <- build_encoder(emb, filters, dropout)

  in_a <- keras_input(shape = c(28, 28, 1))
  in_b <- keras_input(shape = c(28, 28, 1))

  encoded_a <- encoder(in_a)
  encoded_b <- encoder(in_b)

  diff <- layer_subtract(list(encoded_a, encoded_b))

  dist <- layer_lambda(
    diff,
    function(d) {
      op_sqrt(
        op_maximum(
          op_sum(op_square(d), axis = -1L, keepdims = TRUE),
          1e-9
        )
      )
    }
  )

  model <- keras_model(
    inputs = list(in_a, in_b),
    outputs = dist
  )

  model |> compile(
    optimizer = optimizer_adam(learning_rate = lr),
    loss = contrastive_loss(margin)
  )

  model
}
```

# Siamese hyperparameter tuning

```{r}
library(tidyverse); library(pROC)

run_config <- function(emb, filters, dropout, margin, lr, seed) {
  set_random_seed(seed)
  m <- build_siamese(emb = emb, filters = filters, dropout = dropout,
                     margin = margin, lr = lr)
  h <- m |> fit(tr$x, tr$y, epochs = 20, batch_size = 128,
                validation_data = list(va$x, va$y), verbose = 0,
                callbacks = list(callback_early_stopping(
                  monitor = "val_loss", patience = 3, restore_best_weights = TRUE)))
  d <- as.numeric(predict(m, va$x, verbose = 0))
  r <- roc(pairs$val$y, d, levels = c(0, 1), direction = ">", quiet = TRUE)
  fpr <- 1 - r$specificities; fnr <- 1 - r$sensitivities
  list(val_auc = as.numeric(auc(r)),
       val_eer = fpr[which.min(abs(fpr - fnr))],
       epochs  = length(h$metrics$loss),
       history = h)
}

base <- list(emb = 32, filters = 32, dropout = 0.2, margin = 1, lr = 1e-3)

# One setting at a time: each row changes exactly one value
vary <- bind_rows(
  tibble(param = "baseline", value = 0),
  tibble(param = "emb",      value = c(8, 16, 64)),
  tibble(param = "margin",   value = c(0.5, 2)),
  tibble(param = "lr",       value = c(1e-4, 3e-4, 3e-3)),
  tibble(param = "dropout",  value = c(0.5)),
  tibble(param = "filters",  value = c(16, 64))
)

grid <- vary |>
  rowwise() |>
  mutate(cfg = list(modifyList(base,
            if (param == "baseline") list() else setNames(list(value), param)))) |>
  ungroup() |>
  cross_join(tibble(seed = 1:3))

fits <- map2(grid$cfg, grid$seed, \(cfg, s) do.call(run_config, c(cfg, seed = s)))

res <- grid |> select(param, value, seed) |>
  mutate(val_auc = map_dbl(fits, "val_auc"),
         val_eer = map_dbl(fits, "val_eer"),
         epochs  = map_int(fits, "epochs"))

# Summary: mean and sd over seeds
summ <- res |> group_by(param, value) |>
  summarise(auc_mean = mean(val_auc), auc_sd = sd(val_auc),
            eer_mean = mean(val_eer), .groups = "drop") |>
  arrange(desc(auc_mean))
summ

# Sensitivity plot: validation AUC per setting, spread over seeds
ggplot(res, aes(factor(value), val_auc)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point", colour = "red", size = 3) +
  facet_wrap(~param, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(x = "Value", y = "Validation AUC")
```

```{r}
best_cfg <- modifyList(base, setNames(list(best_row$value), best_row$param))
# (if the best row is "baseline", use base as is)

set_random_seed(2026)
best <- do.call(build_siamese, best_cfg)
best |> fit(tr$x, tr$y, epochs = 20, batch_size = 128,
            validation_data = list(va$x, va$y), verbose = 0,
            callbacks = list(callback_early_stopping(
              monitor = "val_loss", patience = 3, restore_best_weights = TRUE)))
```

The strongest previously observed setting increased the learning rate to 0.003 while leaving the remaining baseline parameters unchanged. This produced a validation AUC of approximately 0.984.

#Use test model

```{r}
# Select the threshold using validation data
val_dist <- as.numeric(predict(best, va$x, verbose = 0))

val_roc <- roc(
  pairs$val$y, val_dist,
  levels = c(0, 1),
  direction = ">",
  quiet = TRUE
)

threshold <- as.numeric(
  coords(
    val_roc,
    x = "best",
    best.method = "youden",
    ret = "threshold",
    transpose = FALSE
  )[1]
)

# Classify test pairs using the validation threshold
actual <- pairs$test$y
predicted <- as.integer(test_dist <= threshold)

TP <- sum(predicted == 1 & actual == 1)
TN <- sum(predicted == 0 & actual == 0)
FP <- sum(predicted == 1 & actual == 0)
FN <- sum(predicted == 0 & actual == 1)

sensitivity <- TP / (TP + FN)
specificity <- TN / (TN + FP)

cat("Test AUC:", round(test_auc, 4), "\n")
cat("Test EER:", round(test_eer, 4), "\n")
cat("Test Sensitivity:", round(sensitivity, 4), "\n")
cat("Test Specificity:", round(specificity, 4), "\n")
```

```{r}
  )
```

# Comparison of CNN and Siamese approaches

The CNN and Siamese network address related but different problems. The CNN performs closed-set identification: it predicts which of the 20 known writers produced an image. The Siamese network performs writer verification: it determines whether two samples were produced by the same person.

**what was the accuracy of both neural networks**

These values should not be directly compared as if they represent the same prediction problem. The CNN tests known-writer identification in a new session, while the Siamese model tests matching performance on previously unseen writers.

# Digit and session effects

We can also discuss whether cross-session matching is more difficult than same-session matching and relate this to the CNN results.

# Limitations

Several limitations should be considered. The data are simulated and therefore do not represent all difficulties encountered in real handwriting. Only 20 writers and five digits are represented. The CNN evaluates new sessions from known writers rather than completely new writers. Siamese performance depends on the pair-generation procedure. Neural-network training is stochastic, so small numerical differences may occur between executions.
